subject: geoffrey-hinton
research_tasks: Before quoting any YouTube-sourced line (S08, S10, S11, S12), re-transcribe the exact clip from audio (whisper-cli) and correct auto-caption errors, especially S08 00:02:31 ('successful academic or ailure').

Open the original Axios article (Steve LeVine, September 2017) for Hinton's 'throw it all away and start again' remark on backpropagation; only secondary reproductions were seen. Use it only if opened, as evidence that he would discard his own best-known method.

If the draft uses the 1987 move, find a first-person Hinton account of the Pentagon-funding reason. Otherwise attribute it to the NYT paraphrase (S04) alongside the Reagan/Rosalind (S01) and 'society/basic research' (S17) accounts.
If the hook uses the film Artificial (Mark Rylance reportedly plays Hinton), open a dated primary report confirming casting and release date before writing it; it is not in this evidence record.

Privacy handling: the son's learning difficulties (C14) and Rosalind's medical choices (C18) appear only in Hinton's own words and should stay brief and attributed. Hinton's opinions of Altman and Musk (C24) must be attributed as his view, with context.
Optional current check: coverage of his scheduled Vienna Godel Lecture (TU Wien, announced for 2026-10-23); include only if it adds to the argument.

sources.title: Why the Godfather of A.I. Fears What He's Built
sources.speaker: Geoffrey Hinton (interviewed by Joshua Rothman, The New Yorker)
sources.locator: Full profile; four-day visit to Hinton's Georgian Bay island. Key passages: family-tree/father section ('If you work twice as hard as me'), woodwork vs science ('mostly anxiety'), tree-felling and contractor-notes section, Rosalind and Jackie sections, Boltzmann Machine section, closing 'unplug it' exchange
sources.excerpt: "I've often wondered whether I'd have been happier as an architect, because I didn't have to force myself to do it. Whereas, with science, I've always had to force myself. Because of the family, I had to succeed at it—I had to find a path. There was joy in it, but it was mostly anxiety. Now it's an enormous relief that I've succeeded."
sources.context: Long-form magazine profile built on in-person reporting at Hinton's cottage in 2023, months after he left Google. Hinton's own words are quoted at length; the reporter's scene-setting and interpretations (e.g. 'The tree was an error') are Rothman's, not Hinton's. Canonical page opened by plain curl and checked against a full-text PDF copy; key quotations confirmed on the canonical page. Same visit also yields S02 testimony, so S01 and S02 are not independent of each other.

sources.title: Why the Godfather of A.I. Fears What He's Built (third-party testimony within the profile)
sources.speaker: Yann LeCun; Yoshua Bengio; Rosemary Gartner (quoted by Joshua Rothman)
sources.locator: LeCun: 'Geoff was born into science'; Boltzmann-vs-backprop disagreement; 'I'm not scared of A.I.' Bengio: 'This should not work' review anecdote. Gartner: 'always needs a partner'
sources.excerpt: "Geoff and I disagreed about the Boltzmann Machine," LeCun said. "Geoff thought it was the most beautiful algorithm. I thought it was ugly." ... "I think he's the kind of person who always needs a partner," [Gartner] told me, tenderly.
sources.context: Named testimony from a former student/collaborator who publicly disagrees with Hinton about AI risk (LeCun), a co-laureate (Bengio), and his partner (Gartner). Same article as S01, so it is not independent reporting; it is independent voice.

sources.title: Geoffrey Hinton tells us why he's now scared of the tech he helped build
sources.speaker: Geoffrey Hinton (interviewed by Will Douglas Heaven, MIT Technology Review)
sources.locator: Interview at Hinton's north London house four days before the Google announcement; 'I'm mildly depressed' passage near the optimist/pessimist estimate; Google self-censorship passage near top; 'confabulations' passage mid-article
sources.excerpt: "I want to talk about AI safety issues without having to worry about how it interacts with Google's business," he says. "As long as I'm paid by Google, I can't do that." ... Which is Hinton? "I'm mildly depressed," he says. "Which is why I'm scared."
sources.context: Pre-announcement interview; Hinton paces the room because of his back. Also includes LeCun and Bengio comments on Hinton's risk view. Opened in full.

sources.title: 'The Godfather of AI' Quits Google and Warns of Danger Ahead
sources.speaker: Geoffrey Hinton (interviewed by Cade Metz, The New York Times)
sources.locator: Paragraphs 3-4 (regret / 'normal excuse'); paragraph on Carnegie Mellon and Pentagon funding; closing Oppenheimer paraphrase
sources.excerpt: A part of him, he said, now regrets his life's work. "I console myself with the normal excuse: If I hadn't done it, somebody else would have," Dr. Hinton said ... In the 1980s, Dr. Hinton was a professor of computer science at Carnegie Mellon University, but left the university for Canada because he said he was reluctant to take Pentagon funding.
sources.context: The article that announced his departure. Opened via the Wayback Machine raw capture because nytimes.com is paywalled. The 'regrets his life's work' line is the reporter's paraphrase; Hinton disputed the paper's framing of his reason for leaving the same day (S05).

sources.title: Geoffrey Hinton leaves Google, warns about AI risks (reproduces Hinton's May 1, 2023 tweet)
sources.speaker: Geoffrey Hinton (tweet reproduced by Notebookcheck)
sources.excerpt: "In the NYT today, Cade Metz implies that I left Google so that I could criticize Google. Actually, I left so that I could talk about the dangers of AI without considering how this impacts Google. Google has acted very responsibly."
sources.context: The original post on X was not opened directly; the full text is reproduced verbatim in this opened news report and matches wording quoted by other outlets. Treat the wording as a reproduction.

sources.title: "Godfather of Artificial Intelligence" Geoffrey Hinton on the promise, risks of advanced AI (60 Minutes transcript)
sources.speaker: Geoffrey Hinton (interviewed by Scott Pelley, CBS 60 Minutes)
sources.locator: Transcript: 'At what point did you realize that you were right' exchange; father/beetles exchange; closing 'no regrets' narration
sources.excerpt: Scott Pelley: At what point did you realize that you were right about neural networks and most everyone else was wrong? Geoffrey Hinton: I always thought I was right. ... Geoffrey Hinton: Every morning when I went to school he'd actually say to me, as I walked down the driveway, "get in there pitching and maybe when you're twice as old as me you'll be half as good."
sources.context: Broadcast interview transcript. The father's line differs in wording from the New Yorker version (S01); both are Hinton's recollections. Narration (e.g. 'domineering father', 'no regrets') is CBS's.

sources.title: Geoffrey Hinton – Interview (first-reactions telephone call)
sources.speaker: Geoffrey Hinton (with Adam Smith, Nobel Prize Outreach)
sources.locator: Telephone interview transcript on the page: 'How would you describe yourself?' answer; climate-change comparison
sources.excerpt: GH: I would say I am someone who doesn't really know what field he's in but would like to understand how the brain works. And in my attempts to understand how the brain works, I've helped to create a technology that works surprisingly well.
sources.context: Recorded minutes after the 2 a.m. call in a California hotel. Official transcript on nobelprize.org.

[00:17:57] "so in the end we compromised that I took that half of my share and we used it to set up a prize in his name" ... [00:14:17] "I'm very good at ignoring what other people say"

sources.title: Geoffrey Hinton – Banquet speech
sources.speaker: Geoffrey Hinton
sources.excerpt: "But we now have evidence that if they are created by companies motivated by short-term profits, our safety will not be the top priority. We urgently need research on how to prevent these new beings from wanting to take control. They are no longer science fiction."
sources.context: Official text of his Nobel banquet speech; he spent most of it on risks, not on his own work.

sources.title: Interview with Geoffrey Hinton from the 2024 Nobel Prize banquet (SVT)

[00:01:16] "nobody ever told me I had to do carpentry it's something I always did for myself ... there's never any pressure with carpentry I'm not very good at it but I enjoy it"
sources.context: Short banquet-night interview for Swedish television, posted by the Nobel Prize channel. Auto-caption text; recheck against audio before quoting.

[00:29:44] "another reason is I was just wrong about the speed at which AI systems would be better than Radiologists"

sources.title: Godfather of AI: They Keep Silencing Me But I'm Trying to Warn Them! (The Diary of a CEO)
sources.speaker: Geoffrey Hinton (interviewed by Steven Bartlett)
sources.locator: 00:14:46-00:16:00 (three banks, backup drive); 00:32:01-00:33:07 (guilt, sadness, duty); 00:33:45-00:35:45 (Sutskever, Musk, Altman); 01:11:12-01:12:28 (why he sold to Google); 01:14:55-01:15:52 (why he left Google); 01:22:30-01:24:05 (regret about wife and children); 01:24:59-01:25:13 (depressed/cheerful)

Even if you could get away with it, it just feels wrong to me." ... [00:32:22] "I don't feel particularly guilty about developing AI like 40 years ago" ... [00:33:03] "So, I feel I have a duty now to talk about the risks." ... [01:22:39] "I wish I spent more time with my wife ... and with my children when they were little. I was kind of obsessed with work."
sources.context: 90-minute podcast interview. Captions are cleaner than most auto-captions but remain machine text; recheck exact wording against audio before quoting. Contains a sensitive self-disclosure about his son (01:11:19) and opinions about living people (Musk, Altman).

sources.title: The Secret Auction That Set Off the Race for AI Supremacy (adapted from Genius Makers)
sources.speaker: Cade Metz (reporting, with Hinton quotes)
sources.locator: Opening (back, 'I last sat down in 2005'); room 731 humidifier passage ('old and decrepit'); backpack paragraph; $44 million stop; closing 'right home' paragraph
sources.excerpt: "I didn't want them thinking I was old and decrepit," he says. ... But knowing it wasn't the right thing to do, they didn't. ... Hinton stopped the auction because finding the right home for his research was ultimately more important to him than commanding the maximum price.
sources.context: Book excerpt reconstructing the December 2012 Lake Tahoe auction from interviews. Motive statements ('more important to him') and the backpack decision are Metz's reconstruction, not direct Hinton quotes, except where quoted.

sources.title: From AI to Atari: What it was like to work with Nobel Prize-winner Geoffrey Hinton
sources.speaker: Nick Frosst; Chris Maddison; Kevin Swersky (U of T Department of Computer Science)
sources.locator: Frosst Asteroids/'fever-pitched intensity' paragraph; Maddison 'bursting into a room' paragraph; Swersky office-visit and dishes paragraphs; Frosst desk paragraph
sources.excerpt: "He was famous for bursting into a room and pronouncing that, he now finally, after all these years, understood how the brain worked." (Maddison) ... "It's that fever-pitched intensity, passion and playfulness that he brings to everything" (Frosst)
sources.context: Celebratory university news item collecting former students' anecdotes after the Nobel; affectionate by design, so weigh it as warm testimony, not critical assessment.

sources.title: 'Godfather of AI' warns Congress has 'maybe a year' left to regulate AI
sources.speaker: Geoffrey Hinton (reported by Scott Wong, Sahil Kapur, Brennan Leach and Katie Taylor, NBC News)
sources.locator: Opening paragraphs; 'recursive self-improvement' paragraph; 'little Chernobyl' paragraph
sources.excerpt: "Maybe a year, but not much more than a year," Hinton said Wednesday evening after he and other AI experts huddled with Senate and House lawmakers behind closed doors. ... "It is going to get out of control unless we do something. We need to slow down."
sources.context: Remarks to reporters after a closed-door briefing on Wednesday, September 16, 2026, organized by Sen. Bernie Sanders. The briefing itself was private; these are on-record remarks afterward.

sources.title: Nonprofit group joins Elon Musk's effort to block OpenAI's for-profit transition
sources.speaker: Geoffrey Hinton (statement in Encode press release, quoted by TechCrunch)
sources.locator: Paragraph quoting Hinton's press-release statement (article updated December 30, 2024)
sources.excerpt: "OpenAI was founded as an explicitly safety-focused nonprofit and made a variety of safety-related promises in its charter," Hinton said in a press release. "It received numerous tax and other benefits from its nonprofit status. Allowing it to tear all of that up when it becomes inconvenient sends a very bad message to other actors in the ecosystem."
sources.context: Hinton backed Encode's amicus brief in Musk v. OpenAI. Encode's own release page did not render for text extraction; TechCrunch reproduces the statement.

sources.title: Tech in T.O.: Why Geoffrey Hinton, the 'Godfather of A.I.,' decided to live in Toronto
sources.speaker: Geoffrey Hinton (interviewed by Farah Nasser, Global News)
sources.locator: Quote on why he came to Canada; radiologist quote near end
sources.excerpt: "I came to Canada because I like the society here and because they have very good funding for basic research. It's not very much money, but they give it for basic curiosity driven research as opposed to big applications," he said.
sources.context: Pre-Nobel, pre-safety-turn interview while still at Google. Gives his own short account of the 1987 move without mentioning the Pentagon or Reagan.

sources.title: Geoffrey Hinton | Biography
sources.speaker: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.excerpt: Hinton left the United States for Canada in 1987, a decision fueled by disdain for the U.S. military and the Reagan administration. The majority of American AI research at the time was funded by the U.S. Department of Defense, and Hinton opposed using AI for combat.
sources.context: Reference summary; opened via r.jina.ai text rendering. Secondary characterization of motive, not Hinton's words.

sources.title: Geoffrey E. Hinton's Biographical Sketch
sources.speaker: Geoffrey Hinton (personal university page)
sources.excerpt: Geoffrey Hinton received his BA in Experimental Psychology from Cambridge in 1970 and his PhD in Artificial Intelligence from Edinburgh in 1978. He did postdoctoral work at Sussex University and the University of California San Diego and spent five years as a faculty member in the Computer Science department at Carnegie-Mellon University.
sources.context: Self-maintained official biography; used only for career facts.

claims.claim: Hinton was born on December 6, 1947 (he married Jackie Ford on his 50th birthday, December 6, 1997, and turned 65 during the December 2012 Lake Tahoe auction). He earned a BA in experimental psychology at Cambridge (1970) and a PhD in AI at Edinburgh (1978), spent five years on the Carnegie Mellon faculty, and moved to the University of Toronto in 1987.
claims.inference: Factual biography. The exact birth date is derived from the New Yorker (wedding on his fiftieth birthday, December 6, 1997) and is consistent with Wired (65th birthday at NIPS 2012).
claims.alternative: Wording of degrees and dates should follow S19; omit the full birth date in metadata if a direct source is preferred.

claims.claim: Hinton recalls his father, the entomologist Howard Everest Hinton, setting an impossible standard: 'If you work twice as hard as me, when you're twice as old as I am you might be half as good' (New Yorker), or, in the 60 Minutes telling, said every morning on the driveway: 'get in there pitching and maybe when you're twice as old as me you'll be half as good.' Hinton says his father 'knew a lot more about beetles than he knew about people.'
claims.inference: Establishes a demanding paternal standard Hinton still cites in his seventies. It is consistent with an internalized critical standard (Type 1), but equally with achievement pressure (Type 3) or anxiety (Type 6).
claims.alternative: Two wordings exist; quote each exactly with its source. A childhood standard is context, not proof of type; do not frame it as a causal wound.

claims.claim: Hinton describes science as an obligation and carpentry as freedom: 'with science, I've always had to force myself. Because of the family, I had to succeed at it ... There was joy in it, but it was mostly anxiety. Now it's an enormous relief that I've succeeded.' Of carpentry: nobody ever told him he had to do it, there is 'never any pressure,' and 'I'm not very good at it but I enjoy it.' In Nobel Week he said he knew early that he had to be a successful academic or a failure.
claims.inference: Self-report that his core work ran on pressure and should rather than pure delight. That matters for the type argument: it cuts against a pure Type 5 'retreat into knowledge' reading and fits an internal-standard (1), achievement (3) or anxiety (6) engine.
claims.alternative: Retrospective self-description by a man who, by students' accounts (C07), visibly enjoyed research. 'Successful academic or failure' comes from auto-captions ('ailure'); recheck against audio before quoting.

claims.claim: Hinton frames his independence as being right against a room: sent by atheist parents to a Christian school, he was 'the only person who didn't believe in God and as time went by it turned out I was right'; asked when he realized he was right about neural networks, 'I always thought I was right'; of the decades of doubt, 'It wasn't really faith—it was just completely obvious to me.'
claims.inference: Repeated, cross-context self-description that rightness is something he sees internally and holds against consensus. That fits a Type 1 internal authority and also Type 5 trust in one's own model. It is a weak fit with Type 6, who typically seeks outside confirmation.
claims.alternative: Could be the retrospective confidence of a man proven right, not a lifelong trait. Professional incentive: the 'lone right scientist' story is also a good public narrative.

claims.claim: His standing advice: if an idea seems right and differs from what everyone believes, 'don't give up on it until you figured out why it's wrong' and 'you should just ignore what other people say. I'm very good at ignoring what other people say.'
claims.inference: A repeated rule of conduct (October and December 2024). It shows a standard tested against his own reasoning, not against social approval.
claims.alternative: Generic scientific advice many laureates give; useful for texture more than discrimination. Auto-caption text; recheck against audio.

claims.claim: Hinton defines himself by a question rather than a field: 'I am someone who doesn't really know what field he's in but would like to understand how the brain works.' He traces the question to a school friend's idea about holographic memory around 1965. 60 Minutes reports that his Edinburgh PhD adviser told him to drop neural networks, and that Hinton says he failed to figure out the human mind.
claims.inference: This is the strongest evidence for Type 5: a lifelong driving question about how minds work. Under the Type 1 reading, the question is the vocation and the internal standard is the engine.
claims.alternative: Taken alone, this points to 5. The adviser detail is CBS narration, not a quote.

claims.claim: Former students describe joy and intensity: Chris Maddison says Hinton 'was famous for bursting into a room and pronouncing that, he now finally, after all these years, understood how the brain worked'; Nick Frosst describes 'fever-pitched intensity, passion and playfulness' (he played Asteroids until it damaged a finger) and says Hinton built him a desk; Kevin Swersky says Hinton offered to put him up and go out to buy him dishes.
claims.inference: Independent named testimony of delight in ideas and warmth toward students. This is counterevidence to the 'mostly anxiety' self-report (C03) and to a detached Type 5 caricature, and it is a playful texture a strict Type 1 reading does not predict.
claims.alternative: Celebratory university article; affectionate by design. The Asteroids injury is Frosst's secondhand retelling.

claims.claim: On his island, Hinton keeps correcting the world around him. The New Yorker reports contractors' 'needless mistakes ... that still enrage him today'; almost every room has 'a corrective mini-project' with notes written on the building materials ('Do not prime shelf, prime shelf support'); he is 'always cutting down trees to create more orderly and beautiful tableaus.' The reporter's own gloss on one cedar is 'The tree was an error.'
claims.inference: The clearest non-professional evidence for a Type 1 pattern: anger attached to things done wrong, and repeated effort to bring a place into line with how it should be.
claims.alternative: One reporter's four-day visit. 'The tree was an error' is Rothman's interpretation, not Hinton's words. Precision about building work is also ordinary in an engineer (5) or a homeowner who paid for bad work. The New Yorker appended a correction that an earlier version mischaracterized his tree-felling process; describe the felling only as the corrected text does.

claims.claim: He polices terms: 'We should say "confabulate" ... "Hallucination" is when you think there's sensory input'; MIT Technology Review notes he prefers 'confabulations' 'because it's the correct term in psychology.' He refuses to explain ideas he thinks would be oversimplified: 'It's no use trying to explain complicated ideas that you don't understand. First, you have to understand how something works. Otherwise, you just produce nonsense.'
claims.inference: Precision about correctness. It fits both the Type 1 'get it right' standard and Type 5 mastery-before-speaking, so it does not discriminate on its own.
claims.alternative: Professional habit of a psychologist-trained scientist; not type-specific.

claims.claim: On the day the New York Times announced his departure, Hinton publicly corrected its framing: 'In the NYT today, Cade Metz implies that I left Google so that I could criticize Google. Actually, I left so that I could talk about the dangers of AI without considering how this impacts Google. Google has acted very responsibly.'
claims.inference: A same-day public correction of an error, even one that flattered his own story, defending a former employer. This is a costly-ish act of fairness and accuracy that fits the Type 1 pattern.
claims.alternative: Could also be relationship maintenance with Google (he says he wanted to say good things about it, S03). The tweet is read via a verbatim reproduction, not the original post.

claims.claim: Hinton's stated reasons for leaving Google shifted in emphasis. In May 2023: 'As long as I'm paid by Google, I can't do that.' In June 2025: 'The main reason I left Google was cuz I was 75 and I wanted to retire. I've done a very bad job of that,' the timing was so he could talk freely at an MIT Technology Review conference, Google had encouraged him to stay and work on safety, and staying would have meant self-censorship: 'Even if you could get away with it, it just feels wrong to me.' He also cited making 'many more mistakes when I programmed, which is very annoying.'
claims.inference: The moral reasoning is framed as felt wrongness, not as calculation ('it just feels wrong to me'). That is the language of an internal standard (1). Annoyance at his own declining precision also fits.
claims.alternative: The 2025 account puts age first, so the exit was not purely principled. Retirement plus the wish to speak freely is an ordinary career transition.

claims.claim: Accounts of why Hinton left Carnegie Mellon for Toronto in 1987 differ in emphasis. The NYT says he 'said he was reluctant to take Pentagon funding'. The New Yorker quotes him saying the move was 'partly because Rosalind loathed Ronald Reagan'. In 2019 he told Global News 'I came to Canada because I like the society here and because they have very good funding for basic research'. Britannica summarizes it as 'disdain for the U.S. military and the Reagan administration.'
claims.inference: A principled refusal of military money would be a costly, conscience-led choice consistent with Type 1. But his own accounts mix politics, his wife's views and funding culture.
claims.alternative: Do not present the move as a single heroic refusal. Attribute each reason to its source and note that the Pentagon reason is the NYT's paraphrase of what he said.

claims.claim: At the December 2012 Lake Tahoe auction for DNNresearch, Hinton ran the bidding from Harrah's room 731 while standing (laptop on an upturned trash can), hid his makeshift humidifier from Baidu's Kai Yu ('I didn't want them thinking I was old and decrepit'; 'This is what vice presidents do'), did not open Yu's forgotten backpack 'knowing it wasn't the right thing to do', and stopped the auction at $44 million to sell to Google rather than push the price higher.
claims.inference: The backpack decision and stopping short of the maximum price show rule-keeping and 'right home' over money (consistent with 1). Hiding frailty to protect his image is a point for 3, not 1.
claims.alternative: Metz's reconstruction. The backpack motive and 'right home' explanation are the author's narration; the 'old and decrepit' line is a direct quote. The back problem made China unworkable, which also explains choosing an American buyer.

claims.claim: Hinton says he sold his company to a big company because 'I have a son who has learning difficulties and in order to be sure he would never be out on the street I needed to get several million dollars and I wasn't going to get that as an academic.' He had tried teaching a Coursera course for money first.
claims.inference: A security-and-responsibility motive for the most lucrative decision of his life. It fits a responsible Type 1 or a security-minded Type 6 more than an image-driven Type 3.
claims.alternative: Sensitive: concerns a private living family member. Use only in Hinton's own framing, briefly, or omit. It is a retrospective account given in 2025.

claims.claim: Hinton gave away his Nobel money in two ways. He gave half his share to a Canadian organization that trains people in Indigenous communities to produce safe drinking water, calling it 'crazy' that many Ontario Indigenous communities lack it. With the other half he honored a 1980s agreement with Terry Sejnowski to split any prize one of them won. When Sejnowski declined the money, they set up a prize in Sejnowski's name for young researchers 'with crazy theories of how the brain works um like we were.'
claims.inference: Keeping a forty-year-old informal promise at real cost, and moral indignation ('crazy') at a fixable injustice. These are among the strongest concrete Type 1 data points.
claims.alternative: Generosity and loyalty also fit 2, 6 or 9. Auto-caption text; recheck wording. On October 8, 2024 he had said he had 'no specific plans' beyond charities, including one for neurodiverse young adults.

claims.claim: Hinton has a mordant streak: he tells a reporter that 'Geoff' is an anagram for 'ego fortissimo'; he replied to a long note from a Canadian intelligence agency with 'Snowden is my hero'; he emailed Fox News 'Fox News is an oxy moron'. At his Nobel press conference he joked he was not sure 'how a neural network could get rid of Doug Ford.'
claims.inference: Irreverent, anti-authority wit. Sharp one-liners fit a Type 1 critic's dry edge and a counterphobic Type 6, and the playfulness also brushes Type 7.
claims.alternative: Humor is weak type evidence; much of it is public performance by an articulate Englishman.

claims.claim: Remembering his father forbidding him to study biology on Communist ideological grounds, Hinton said: 'I hate faiths of all kinds.'
claims.inference: Strong aversion to belief held without evidence. That fits an internal standard of correctness (1), skepticism (6) or a reasoning-first temperament (5).
claims.alternative: One remark in context of a specific childhood conflict.

claims.claim: Hinton's grief has two contrasting shapes. When his second wife Rosalind, a molecular biologist, chose homeopathy over chemotherapy for ovarian cancer and asked him to sell their house to fund treatment, he 'drew the line' to protect the children, and he still seems 'angry, guilty, wounded, mystified'; she died in 1994 when the children were five and three. Of his third wife Jackie, who died of pancreatic cancer in 2018, he says she was 'incredibly brave and incredibly rational'. He draws the lesson for AI himself: 'We can't be in denial ... We have to be real.'
claims.inference: Shows how he responds to irrationality in someone he loves: anger and a firm line set for the children's sake. It also shows him generalizing grief into a principle about facing reality, which reads as both 1 (the right response) and 5 (the rational stance).
claims.alternative: Highly sensitive: a deceased private person's medical choices, told only from Hinton's side. Use sparingly, attribute, and never characterize Rosalind beyond what he said. He has also said 'She hurt people by failing to accept that she was going to die'; quoting it requires care.

claims.claim: Asked what he would have done differently, Hinton said: 'I wish I spent more time with my wife ... and with my children when they were little. I was kind of obsessed with work.'
claims.inference: Work obsession at a family cost, with late regret. It fits a duty-and-standard engine (1), mind-absorption (5) or achievement (3) equally; this is the cost side of the pattern, not a discriminator.
claims.alternative: Retrospective emotion in a podcast setting; common regret among high achievers.

claims.claim: Hinton's statements on regret and guilt vary. The NYT (May 2023) reported 'A part of him, he said, now regrets his life's work,' quoting 'I console myself with the normal excuse: If I hadn't done it, somebody else would have.' In late 2023 he sent a journalist Edith Piaf's 'Non, Je Ne Regrette Rien' as a one-liner, and 60 Minutes reported he has no regrets. In 2025 he said 'I don't feel particularly guilty about developing AI like 40 years ago' but 'I feel I have a duty now to talk about the risks.'
claims.inference: Most of his statements converge on no personal guilt for past work plus a forward-looking duty. Duty-without-guilt fits a principled reformer. The relative absence of self-reproach is counterevidence to a classic Type 1 inner critic.
claims.alternative: The NYT 'regrets' line is the reporter's paraphrase, which Hinton's later statements soften. Present this as a change over time, not a contradiction to exploit.

claims.claim: Hinton describes himself as temperamentally gloomy and takes concrete precautions: 'I'm mildly depressed ... Which is why I'm scared' (2023). 'When I'm feeling slightly depressed, I think people are toast. AI is going to take over. When I'm feeling cheerful, I think we'll figure out a way' (2025). He spreads his and his children's money across three Canadian banks against a cyberattack and backs up his laptop to a disk drive.
claims.inference: This is the strongest support for a Type 6 alternative: anticipatory worry plus practical hedging against specific threats.
claims.alternative: He presents the gloom as calibration ('the mildly depressed person ... usually right'), not as dread. Hedging against a modeled risk is also what a Type 5 or 1 would do once convinced.

claims.claim: Since leaving Google Hinton has spent himself on public advocacy rather than retirement. In October 2024 he said: 'I'm 76 and I'm not going to do much more Frontier research ... I'm going to spend my time advocating uh for people to work on safety.' On September 16, 2026, after a closed-door briefing for lawmakers organized by Sen. Bernie Sanders, he told reporters Congress had 'Maybe a year, but not much more than a year' and said 'We need to slow down.'
claims.inference: A repeated, costly choice of public duty over rest. It is central to the Type 1 reading (reformer acting on a 'should') and harder to square with a withdrawing Type 5, though a healthy 5 moving toward 8 could also explain it.
claims.alternative: Late-career public roles are also shaped by demand: Nobel prestige makes him a sought-after voice. Lawmakers' interest, not only his drive, puts him in the room.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check when Congress passes or kills AI-safety legislation (e.g. the AI Kill Switch Act), or when Hinton gives a major new policy speech or retires from public advocacy; review by 2027-09-16 when his 'maybe a year' window lapses.

claims.claim: In his December 10, 2024 Nobel banquet speech Hinton spent his time on risks: 'we now have evidence that if they are created by companies motivated by short-term profits, our safety will not be the top priority. We urgently need research on how to prevent these new beings from wanting to take control.'
claims.inference: He used the profession's highest ceremonial platform for a warning rather than a victory lap. That is consistent with duty over image.
claims.alternative: An audience-aware choice; the Nobel committee had already linked the prize to safety discussion.

claims.claim: At his Nobel press conference Hinton said: 'I'm particularly proud of the fact that one of my students fired Sam Altman.' Asked to elaborate, he said OpenAI had been set up with a big emphasis on safety and that Altman over time turned out to be 'much less concerned with safety than with profits.' In 2025 he said Ilya Sutskever 'has a good moral compass' and that Elon Musk 'has no moral compass'. Of Altman he said 'We'll see. I don't know Sam.'
claims.inference: He makes blunt public moral judgments of powerful people. That fits a Type 1 judging mind (and an 8-like bluntness), and he declines to judge someone he doesn't know.
claims.alternative: These are opinions about living people. Attribute them as Hinton's view; if used, add separately sourced context on the November 2023 board firing and Altman's reinstatement, and any OpenAI response. The auto-captions spell the name 'Alman'.

claims.claim: Hinton backed Encode's amicus brief opposing OpenAI's for-profit conversion (December 2024): 'OpenAI was founded as an explicitly safety-focused nonprofit and made a variety of safety-related promises in its charter ... Allowing it to tear all of that up when it becomes inconvenient sends a very bad message to other actors in the ecosystem.'
claims.inference: He objects to a promise being broken when keeping it becomes inconvenient. That is the same principle as his own Sejnowski agreement (C15). The rule-and-promise concern is a Type 1 signature.
claims.alternative: Policy position shared by many safety advocates; may reflect alliance-building as much as temperament.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check if OpenAI's corporate structure changes again or the Musk v. OpenAI litigation produces a final ruling.

claims.claim: Hinton admits error plainly: of his 2016 prediction that AI would be reading all radiology scans by now, 'that prediction was wrong I was a bit over enthusiastic' and 'I was just wrong about the speed'. On AI timelines, 'I thought it was 30 to 50 years or even longer away. Obviously, I no longer think that'; and 'I have suddenly switched my views.'
claims.inference: He updates easily and without visible self-flagellation. That reads as a model-updater (Type 5), and it is counterevidence for the harsh self-criticism often associated with Type 1.
claims.alternative: Admitting error is also a credibility tool for a public warner; ease here does not show his private reaction.

claims.claim: Hinton theorizes emotion: 'I think feelings are counterfactual statements about what would have caused an action ... Feelings are just a way of talking about inclinations to action.' He told SVT that AI will have emotions such as fear, because a small battle robot needs to run from a big one.
claims.inference: Translating feelings into mechanism is a classic Type 5 move: understanding emotion by modeling it. This is counterevidence for the leading Type 1 read.
claims.alternative: It is also simply his scientific position on AI and minds, held for professional reasons.

claims.claim: Hinton loved the Boltzmann Machine for its beauty: 'It should be true ... If I was God, I'd make it true.' Of backpropagation: 'It's so unsatisfying intellectually ... Unfortunately, it just works better.' LeCun: 'Geoff thought it was the most beautiful algorithm. I thought it was ugly.' Bengio recalls Hinton writing 'This should not work' on his master's thesis, which worked anyway.
claims.inference: 'Should be true' idealism about how the world ought to work, set aside when evidence says otherwise. This is a 1-flavored idealism disciplined by evidence; it also fits 5's aesthetic of elegant models.
claims.alternative: The quotes are about algorithms, not morality; reading 'should' as typological is interpretive.

claims.claim: Hinton says his turn to AI safety came from understanding, not alarm. His closest thing to a eureka moment was Google's PaLM explaining why a joke was funny, coupled with realizing how much better digital systems are than analog ones at sharing what they learn. He had earlier been astonished when ChatGPT explained his 'Fox News is an oxy moron' joke.
claims.inference: The fear follows a model conclusion. That is a point for 5 (and for 1's evidence-first rightness) against an anxiety-first Type 6 reading.
claims.alternative: He also says he wishes he had worried sooner (S08), so the earlier absence of worry may reflect field incentives.

claims.claim: Peers disagree about his risk view but not his seriousness. LeCun: 'I'm not scared of A.I. ... the desire to dominate has nothing to do with intelligence—it has to do with testosterone.' Bengio says he sees no solid argument that the risks Geoff describes are absent. Partner Rosemary Gartner: 'I think he's the kind of person who always needs a partner.'
claims.inference: Independent voices that test his stance. Gartner's remark cuts against a self-sufficient, low-need Type 5 caricature.
claims.alternative: LeCun's disagreement is about AI, not Hinton's character. Gartner is an intimate, affectionate witness.

claims.claim: Because of a back injury he traces to lifting a space heater as a teenager, Hinton has largely stopped sitting: 'I last sat down in 2005 ... and it was a mistake.' He has not sat for more than an hour since 2005. He works at standing desks, kneels to eat, lies down in cars, and travels by train and bus rather than commercial flights. His comment: 'If you let it completely control your life ... it doesn't give you any problems.'
claims.inference: Decades of disciplined self-management under constraint, delivered with dry humor. It is a vivid, durable detail, not strongly type-discriminating.
claims.alternative: Travel details come from 2012-2023 reporting; whether he still avoids commercial flights today is unverified, so do not state current habits without a check.

claims.claim: Hinton has collected the field's top honors: the 2018 ACM Turing Award with Yoshua Bengio and Yann LeCun (sources variously date it 2018 or 2019; it is the 2018 award, conferred in 2019), and the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics, shared with John Hopfield. The Nobel news reached him by phone around 1-2 a.m. in a California hotel. His first thought was that it might be a spoof, and he later ran a mock statistical argument that he was more likely dreaming.
claims.inference: Biographical anchors. The 'spoof call' and dream-probability reasoning are characteristic analytic humor.
claims.alternative: None; factual. The New Yorker's 'That June' after Jackie's April 2018 death conflicts with the 2019 conferral; follow the 2018-award / 2019-conferral framing.

claims.claim: Hinton's view on slowing AI changed. In 2023 he declined to sign the six-month pause letter ('China's not going to stop developing it for six months'), and in October 2024 he said 'I've never recommended slowing the advancement of AI because I don't think that's feasible'. In September 2026 he told reporters 'We need to slow down.'
claims.inference: A real change of position as his timelines shortened. This is evidence of updating on evidence rather than holding a fixed creed.
claims.alternative: The 2026 quote is a post-briefing remark to reporters; it may be rhetorical rather than a formal policy shift.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check if Hinton endorses or rejects a specific pause or moratorium proposal, or signs a new public statement on slowing AI.

claims.claim: Hinton measures himself against his father and enjoys being surpassed by students. Recruiting, he would ask advisers of job candidates 'But are they better than you?' He wonders whether his competitive father would have been happy to see him succeed, 'Because now I've been more successful than he was.' He mentioned to 60 Minutes that he has more academic citations than his father.
claims.inference: Comparison with his father is a live theme (a 3 or 1 marker). Delight in being surpassed by students cuts against status competition.
claims.alternative: The citations remark is CBS narration ('he happened to mention').

claims.claim: In his Nobel Week interview Hinton said he wished he had worried sooner: 'I would like to have been concerned about this existential threat sooner ... I always thought super intelligence was a long way off and we could worry about it later.'
claims.inference: A self-correction about his own past priorities, framed as hindsight rather than guilt. This is consistent with duty-without-guilt (C20).
claims.alternative: Auto-caption text; recheck wording against audio before quoting.

type_hypothesis.against: The most obvious read of Hinton is Type 5, and real evidence supports it. He defines himself by a question ('would like to understand how the brain works', C06). Students describe joy in ideas, not duty (C07). He theorizes feelings as mechanisms (C27), updates calmly when wrong (C26), and reached his AI fear through a model of digital versus analog learning (C29). The Type 1 reading must also absorb several things. His treatment of his own past is relatively guilt-free (C20), which is unusual for a 1's inner critic. He is playful and irreverent (C07, C16). He calls science 'mostly anxiety' (C03), which fits Type 6 or 3 as well as 1. He hedges concretely against threats (three banks, C21). And he hid his frailty during the 2012 auction to protect his image (C13).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 5, the investigator: a lifelong drive to understand how minds work, pursued for fifty years against a dismissive field, with his worth anchored in having the right model. This reading explains why he says he 'doesn't really know what field he's in' and why his warnings come from analysis rather than alarm. It also explains his insistence on understanding before explaining (C09), his intellectualizing of emotion (C27), his willingness to abandon methods that don't fit the brain (C28), his work absorption at his family's expense (C19) and the island retreat. A Type 6 reading (anxiety plus contrarian distrust of authority, C17, C21, C16) was also considered and ranked third: Hinton's certainty is self-generated ('it was just completely obvious to me', C04), not tested against allies or authorities.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What Hinton does after he sees something is wrong. A Type 5 typically understands an error and conserves himself. Across domains and decades, Hinton instead attaches heat and a 'should' to the error and acts to correct it, often at a cost. He publicly corrected the NYT's framing of his exit the same day, defending Google (C10). He left a paid post because staying quiet 'just feels wrong to me' (C11). He kept a forty-year-old promise to split his Nobel money (C15). He condemned OpenAI for tearing up its promises 'when it becomes inconvenient' (C25). He gave up retirement to advocate as a 'duty' (C22). At home, contractors' errors 'still enrage him' and every room carries corrective notes (C08). Limits: the home details rest on one reporter's visit, the 1987 Pentagon refusal is reported rather than quoted (C12), and many principled people of any type keep promises.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: Several things stay unexplained by the Type 1 reading. One is the exuberant, almost Seven-like delight students describe (bursting into rooms to announce he finally understood the brain). Another is his easy, guilt-free admissions of error, together with 'Non, Je Ne Regrette Rien'. A third is his self-report that science was 'mostly anxiety', which a Type 6 reading explains as well. Finally, the image-protective concealment of his illness at the 2012 auction looks more like Type 3. No wing or subtype is proposed; 1w2 (public duty, warmth to students) and 1w9 (dry detachment, island life) both have some support and neither is defensible from this record.
